REFUTED: removing the casts in Chunks costs 5x. ArraySeq.untagged.newBuilder[A] needs no ClassTag AND answers a typed ArraySeq[A] (backed by Object[], verified), so the asInstanceOf in Chunks.wrap CAN be deleted — it is not a language limitation. Measured per 64-element chunk: array-fill-then-cast 64.4±0.3ns, untagged builder 306.6±78ns; the half-full case (what fromIterator does at the end of a source) 37.8±0.2 vs 157.8±40. At ~16 chunks per 1000 elements that is ~4us on the 16.9us chunked stream lane, about 23%. ALSO: typedArray (a ClassTag'd Array[String], which the generic producers cannot have) is 69.1±3.9 — the SAME as the cast version, so the cast itself costs nothing at runtime. It buys the absence of a ClassTag in every producer's signature, for free

The 28 casts in the chunk-building family became 3, all in ChunkBuf.scala, at NO measured cost: okayChunksTransform 16.891±0.519us against the 16.9 recorded before, okayChunks 22.9 against 23.6. The consolidation is an OPAQUE TYPE over the same Array[AnyRef] the producers were allocating by hand, so it erases to exactly that — no object, no indirection. A real class was 2x (161 vs 78 per chunk) because escape analysis does not remove it; ArraySeq.untagged.newBuilder, which needs no casts at all, was 5x

NOT a speed question: a ClassTag'd Array[String] is 65.7ns against the cast version's 76.7 — the same. Tried threading ClassTag through instead of casting, and it widens in three waves: (1) the leaf builders generate/fromIterator/rechunk/mapChunk/filterChunk/Pipe.chunked, (2) the public combinators they back — Chunks.map, .filter, nats, fibs — so every user's generic function over Chunks[A] needs the evidence, (3) Pipeline.chunks, where it STOPS: the reified operator tree has existential intermediates (case Mapped[A, B](src: Pipeline[A], f: A => B)) and no ClassTag[A] can be recovered at a Mapped node. It would have to be STORED in the tree — a data-structure change, produced at every site that builds a pipeline. Three casts in ChunkBuf.scala is the cheaper side

REFUTED, and UNSOUND. type Backing[A] = A match {case Long => Array[Long]; ... case _ => Array[AnyRef]} plus inline erasedValue[A] match does specialize with no ClassTag: MatchBuf[Long](4) allocates long[]. Through a GENERIC function (what map/generate/fromIterator are) A is abstract, the inline match cannot reduce, and it falls to Array[AnyRef] — same non-specialization as today. But the TYPE still reduces inside the defining scope where the extensions live, so Backing[Long] is Array[Long] while the value is Object[]: ClassCastException [Ljava.lang.Object; cannot be cast to [J. Strictly worse than the cast. The condition it needs (element type static at the allocation site) is the condition Staged already exploits, at 10x (1.6us vs 16.9), not a few percent

IT WORKS, unlike the match type. Choose only the BACKING, never the type: ArraySeq.ofLong and an ofRef of boxed Longs are both honest ArraySeq[Long], so inline + summonFrom[ClassTag[A]] can pick one and neither branch lies. Verified: specializes at a static A (long[]/int[]/double[]/char[]/String[]), composes across inline hops, and falls back CORRECTLY at the first non-inline generic boundary. Worth, on 64 Longs unboxed vs boxed: map 14.6 vs 117.8ns (8.1x), construction 17.2 vs 91.5 (5.3x), summing read 8.7 vs 18.3 (2.1x). java.lang.Long caches only -128..127 so nearly every element is an allocation — the same experiment on Char was 8%, which is why this needed measuring per type. ChunkBuf.tabulate ships; making Chunks.map/filter inline to reach it is the open question

END TO END: okayChunksTransform 13.256±0.763us against 16.891±0.519 measured before specialization — 21% off the lane the project quotes against fs2 and ZStream. Mechanism: inline entry point + ordinary recursion, with the per-chunk worker (ChunkBuf.mapper/filterer/filler) specialized ONCE at the call site and handed to the recursion as a value, so the ClassTag rides in its closure and every chunk is unboxed, not only the first. map, filter, generate and ofSpecialized all take it; fromIterator and rechunk hold a buffer across pulls from an external source and stay untyped. okayChunks (the non-transform lane) 24.8 vs 23.6 — within noise, it does not use the specialized path

REFUTED, and the slowest of every alternative tried. ArrayBuffer per 64 elements: 382.6±36ns ending in ArraySeq.from, 326.3±8 ending in toArray, against the shipped ChunkBuf's 84.2±17. Three costs stack: a capacity check per append, an Array[AnyRef] backing that boxes primitives whatever A is, and a COPY to reach the immutable chunk (the internal array is private, so it cannot be handed over). The third is the worst: always boxed, it would also foreclose the ClassTag specialization, which is worth 21% on the stream lane. Full table now in ChunkBuf's doc: opaque 84ns, real class 2x, untagged builder 3.2x, ArrayBuffer 3.9-4.5x

The ClassTag rides WITH the existential: case Mapped[A, B](src, f)(using val tag: ClassTag[B]) captures it where the node is built and B is still concrete, and Pipeline.chunks reconstructs the specializing mapper from it. This was the wall that stopped ClassTag threading three commits ago, and storing the tag in the node is what gets past it. Proven by test — a reified AND optimized pipeline now yields long[] chunks. On the benchmark it is small: interpretedTree 14.88+-1.07 against 15.9 recorded in an earlier session, and specializing Chunks.range's source as well did not move it further (15.05 -> 14.88, within error). The 8x measured per chunk does not reach this lane, which is dominated by Free stepping, the filter and the fold. Recorded so nobody expects it to

REFUTED, and UNSOUND — the fifth alternative tried. opaque type ChunkBuf[A] = Array[A] with an inline apply + summonFrom compiles, specializes a direct ChunkBuf[Long](n) to long[], and falls back to Object[] for a generic caller which reads back correctly. Then hand the generically-built buffer to code that knows A = Long: ClassCastException [Ljava.lang.Object; cannot be cast to [J, because inside the defining file ChunkBuf[Long] REDUCES to Array[Long] and that is false for what the fallback built. Same failure as the match type, same cause: the BUFFER's type made to depend on A. The shipped specialization avoids it by answering Chunk[A] = ArraySeq[A], a type that tolerates either backing honestly

The idea that WORKED where two type-level ones did not: an EXISTENTIAL backing (Array[?]) with the ClassTag beside it. The backing type claims nothing, so nothing can be false about it — which is exactly what crashed both opaque ChunkBuf[A]=Array[A] and the match type when a generically built buffer met code that knew A=Long. Writing dispatches via ScalaRunTime.array_update. Per 64 elements at Long: 44.7 vs 92.3 boxed (2.07x); at String 67.5 vs 63.8, so the dispatch is free where there is nothing to unbox. tabulate is still better where it applies (14.9) — this is for where it cannot: fromIterator and rechunk hold the buffer across pulls from an external source, and both now specialize. End to end okayChunksTransform 12.477+-0.462 against 16.891 before any of this work, okayChunks 22.0 against 23.6

SIMPLIFICATION that was also a speedup. Two buffer types (opaque ChunkBuf over Array[AnyRef], plus a TaggedBuf class over Array[?]) collapsed into ONE: opaque type ChunkBuf[A] = Array[?]. Opaque so there is no runtime object (a value class would nearly do; opaque has no boxing corner cases), existential so the type claims nothing and the two type-level attempts' unsoundness cannot recur. apply is inline + summonFrom, so a plain ChunkBuf[Long](n) is now specialized BY DEFAULT: 14.8ns against 92.3 before, and indistinguishable from the tabulate that used to be needed for it (14.7) — so tabulate was deleted, it had no production caller left.
